extracted.intended_audience: Students currently enrolled at any ABA law school who wish to submit a Comment to the Columbia Law Review
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for law students submitting short student-authored legal scholarship (Comments) to the Columbia Law Review’s Notes Committee, including eligibility, scope, formatting, anonymous review, and submission procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Students currently enrolled at any ABA law school may submit a short piece of student scholarship for consideration by the Columbia Law Review’s Notes Committee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submissions must be student-authored. If selected for publication, the Comment will be published on CLR Forum (the Review’s online component).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a Comment
rubrics_metrics.description: A Comment is a short piece of student-authored legal scholarship discussing a recent and important judicial decision, analyzing a development in the law, or advancing a novel legal idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While often a “case Comment,” the Review also considers Comments about new or pending legislation, recent executive or administrative action, or new takes on existing doctrines. You can adapt prior research (e.g., seminar papers) but would likely need substantial adaptation for a suitable Comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: For a Comment to be successful, the problem or issue discussed must be novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not enough to write about a new decision or development that simply perpetuates a problem that has already been discussed or written about at length in other legal scholarship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and focus (conciseness)
rubrics_metrics.description: By virtue of their very focused scope, Comments are shorter than Notes, typically about fifteen pages long.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments take a clear position within limited space and must recognize all sides of the issue within the limits imposed by brevity. All things being equal, a shorter Comment is a stronger Comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Position and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments take a clear position on the case or issue they address, but in a respectful and non-confrontational way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful Comment articulates a position forcefully while treating contrary arguments seriously and respectfully, which lends credibility to the author’s position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional Comments identify a specific, very recent, notable case; detail the decision; and advise on implications, but the Review also considers development-oriented pieces (legislation, executive/administrative action, new doctrinal takes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors may write beyond judicial decisions to other legal developments; the key is a recent, important development or a novel idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length limits for publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Typically, Comments are around fifteen double-spaced pages when they are published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At the submission stage the Review may select pieces that are slightly longer but is unlikely to publish a submission exceeding twenty-five pages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting — main text
rubrics_metrics.description: Your above-the-line text must be in 12-point, double-spaced, Times New Roman font.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Word’s formatting features (e.g., cross-reference) for internal references to help keep supra/infra references correct when moving text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting — footnotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Footnoted text must be in 11-point, single-spaced, Times New Roman font.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow consistent footnote formatting per Bluebook and CLR preferences (see CLR Style Guide).

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation style
rubrics_metrics.description: For citations, please follow the Bluebook.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult the CLR Style Guide to adhere to the Review’s stylistic preferences; the Style Guide can be provided on request.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Word cross-references
rubrics_metrics.description: We suggest using the 'cross-reference' feature in Word when making references to text within your Comment ('supra' or 'infra' references).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using cross-references makes it easy to update internal references if you move sections around.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymous review process
rubrics_metrics.description: The Review uses an anonymous review process for student-authored works: the Notes Committee does not know the identity of any author whose piece it considers for publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any member of the Notes Committee who knows who wrote a Comment being deliberated on will recuse themselves and not vote. To preserve anonymity, authors should refrain from discussing their Comments with any CLS student on the Review’s 2026-2027 Notes Committee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of identifying information
rubrics_metrics.description: The Comment file should be devoid of any identifying information (name, UNI, etc.), so that the Notes Committee may consider it pursuant to its anonymous review process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Staff of the Review will redact identifying information before communicating with the Notes Committee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission format and method
rubrics_metrics.description: Submit a final draft of your piece, along with an up-to-date preemption check, as a single Word document to comments@columbialawreview.org.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must be emailed by the stated deadline and sent as one Word file (no multiple attachments indicated).

rubrics_metrics.name: Deadline and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Submissions are due Wednesday, July 1, 2026, at 10 a.m. ET.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Late submissions would not meet the stated deadline; include the required preemption check and ensure anonymity before submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption check requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The submission must include an up-to-date preemption check.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preemption check must use the template provided in the Comments Manual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation / double-dipping policy
rubrics_metrics.description: You can often adapt other research you have done at your law school (e.g., research for a professor or a seminar paper) into a Comment; however, a research memorandum or seminar paper would likely need to be substantially adapted in order to be a suitable Comment for publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check with the Registrar and your professors about whether it is appropriate to 'double-dip' research. Columbia Law School does not permit using the same work product for multiple course credits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Committee communication and redaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Staff of the Review will redact identifying information before communicating with the Notes Committee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If authors need to contact the Review about the Comments Program, send questions to comments@columbialawreview.org; staff will handle redaction prior to review.
